analysis.one_liner: Reduces the minimum wage the government requires growers to pay H-2A guest farmworkers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee with one cosponsor; no committee or floor action has followed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill changes how the government sets the 'adverse effect wage rate,' the wage floor that farms must pay to hire H-2A guest workers from abroad. It directs the Labor Department to stop using the USDA's farm wage survey and instead use the Bureau of Labor Statistics' broader occupational wage survey. Because the broader survey counts a wider mix of jobs and generally reports lower pay for field work, this would lower the wage floor farms must meet. It also lets immigration officials start processing H-2A petitions before the Labor Department finishes certifying that enough U.S. workers are not available.
analysis.who_benefits: Farms and agricultural labor contractors that hire H-2A guest workers, because the required wage floor would drop, cutting their largest cost. Growers argue the current rate overstates market wages and makes crops uneconomical to harvest.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Labor Department to set the H-2A adverse effect wage rate using the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics survey instead of the current method [S2].
Allows the Department of Homeland Security to begin processing an H-2A worker petition while the Labor Department is still reviewing the labor certification, which can speed hiring [S2].

analysis.who_pays: H-2A guest workers, who would be required to be paid less, and U.S. farmworkers, whose wages are benchmarked against the same rate, so a lower floor pulls their pay down too.

drawbacks.text: The bill's stated purpose is to lower the required wage rate for H-2A workers; the required rate is also the practical benchmark for U.S. farmworkers' pay in many jobs, so a lower floor reduces pay for the people the bill's title says it protects [S2].
Speeding petition processing before the Labor Department finishes its labor certification weakens the check on whether U.S. workers were available for the job [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go entirely to agricultural employers through lower labor costs, while the wage floor that protects both guest workers and U.S. farmworkers is cut. Growers' cost argument is real — the current rate has risen sharply — but the bill addresses it entirely on the backs of the workers rather than through subsidies or other means.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was just introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no action and only one cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Monica De La Cruz introduced the bill on December 18, 2025, with Rep. Maria Salazar, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1].
The bill has one cosponsor, a Republican [S3].
No further action has been taken since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet: the bill has not advanced, so farmworkers have lost nothing and growers have gained nothing. If it stayed dormant, the current wage method simply remains in place.

for.name: Rep. Monica De La Cruz
for.role: Sponsor, House Agriculture Committee member from Texas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to change how the H-2A wage floor is calculated

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred. So far the bill's two names are both Republicans, and it has drawn no cosponsors from the other party [S3].

industries.industry: Fruit, vegetable, and other labor-intensive farms hiring H-2A workers
industries.note: The bill lowers the wage floor these employers must pay guest workers, cutting their biggest cost. The saving comes directly out of farmworkers' pay.

industries.industry: Farm labor contractors and H-2A recruiting agencies
industries.note: Faster concurrent petition processing and a lower wage floor make it cheaper and quicker to place guest workers.
The required wage rate is the floor guest workers must be paid and the reference point for U.S. farmworkers' wages; both would see pay pressure downward.

analysis.trajectory: Bills with a single sponsor and one cosponsor referred to Judiciary rarely reach the floor, especially late in the first session. The most likely path is that it stays in committee unless it is attached to a larger farm or immigration package. Grower groups have sought this change before, so it could reappear in a broader bill.
